Never, on any timescale that matters. The premise is a myth.

At room temperature, glass is an amorphous solid, not a slow liquid. Its viscosity is so high that calculations (Zanotto, 1998, and later refinements) put the time for visible flow in window glass at far longer than the age of the universe. Your windows won't sag; the frames, putty, and seals will fail long before the glass moves.

Old church windows are uneven because of how they were made. Medieval and early modern glass was often crown glass, spun from a molten blob into a disc that came out thicker toward the center. Panes cut from it varied in thickness, and glaziers usually set the heavier edge at the bottom for stability. Surveys of old windows also find panes installed thick-side-up or sideways, which wouldn't happen if gravity had caused the unevenness. And ancient Roman glass and centuries-old telescope lenses show no flow, even though optics would reveal deformation far smaller than anything you could see.
